name: NFW Elite Championship
notes: Named by the fed's own championship ledger only in passing, in the National Championship's own closing note; the belt has no lineage of its own on that page, and what survives of its custody comes from the fed's own served show documents.

events.title: nfw-triple-crown
events.note: Folded into the new Triple Crown Championship at Reloaded 11, having sat vacant since a 2010 tournament the record never finishes.

epitaph: An interfed belt whose whole custody the record can only half account for. Steve Knox is already carrying it when NFW's own cameras first find it, at Crash TV 46 in August 2008; the show's own account of how he got it has him beating three other promotions' champions to do it, none of it staged on an NFW card. Wyatt Connors took it off him at Supercrash II two months later, in a segment the broadcast reported rather than showed. After that the belt goes quiet: by July 2010 the fed is describing it as vacated and crediting the vacancy back to Knox rather than to Connors, and running an interfed tournament to fill it whose first round is the only round that survives. It was revived on paper in January 2012 for the sole purpose of being merged into the Triple Crown Championship three months later. Where the chain breaks, it breaks in the fed's own record, not in this one.

name: NFW Mid-Atlantic Championship
notes: Transcribed from the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).
epitaph: A regional championship that lasted nine months. Alex Wylde beat Armando Montezuma in the final of a sixteen-man tournament to win it at Banned 4 Life in June 2001; Pat Black took it that November. The ledger records the end as an act of the fed's own authority rather than a match: Commissioner Michael Manson fired Black and discontinued the title on 17 March 2002, at Impact 2.

events.note: Commissioner Michael Manson fired Pat Black and discontinued the title at Impact 2, per the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).

name: NFW National Championship
notes: Transcribed from the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).
epitaph: A second singles championship the fed introduced at Supercrash I in February 2008, decided in a double-elimination tournament that Teresa Quaranta won over Rook Black. Steve Knox took it that August and Rook Black got it back at Supercrash II, holding it 923 days. Supercrash III in San Antonio put three reigns on it in one night: Thirteen won it and was unmasked on the spot as High Flyer, Doc Curiosity took it from him, and Rook Black took it back. The ledger closes on that second Rook Black reign with a note that the belt became the Triple Crown Championship, merged with the Pure and Elite Championships, after he beat Deacon and Stalker at Reloaded 11 in April 2012.

events.title: nfw-triple-crown
events.note: The fed's own ledger, in this title's own closing note: the National Championship "became Triple Crown Championship (Merged with Pure & Elite Championship) after Rook Black defeated Deacon & Stalker at Reloaded 11 (04/20/12)."

name: NFW Pure Championship
notes: Named by the fed's own championship ledger only in passing, in the National Championship's own closing note; the belt has no lineage of its own on that page, and the reigns below come from the fed's own served show documents instead.

events.title: nfw-triple-crown
events.note: Folded into the new Triple Crown Championship at Reloaded 11, on a presidential order announced three months earlier at Supercrash IV.

epitaph: A championship NFW's own ledger never gave a lineage to. Bloodhunt unveiled the belt at the 2010 opening night in Philadelphia after losing to Sean Stevens, crowned Stevens its first champion on the spot, called him drug-free and demanded Olympic-style testing of anyone who wanted it — an argument aimed squarely at the World Champion of the day. Stevens held it into 2011 and was suspended with it; Troy Windham then had Bobby Jack Windham named champion as one of the terms of the Supercrash III deal, on the grounds that no Windham was purer. Legion won it in a four-corners match at Reloaded X by falling on an unconscious champion, and Stalker took it from him at Supercrash IV in a chain match while Legion's own valet worked against him. Three months later it stopped existing, merged into the Triple Crown. The fed's own championship history lists none of that: the belt appears there once, in another title's closing note.

name: NFW Television Championship
notes: Transcribed from the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).
epitaph: The fed's own working belt, twice discontinued and twice brought back. Tempesta Del Fuerte won it out of a one-night sixteen-man tournament at Impact 4 in July 2002; Steel Viper took it at Futureshock the following month and the title was retired at the end of that same night. It returned at Wrestlebowl II in May 2007 with co-champions — Shawn Jessica Hart and Joe The Plumber simultaneously won the battle royal that decided it, Hart disappeared the next night, and Joe was declared sole champion. Impulse won the vacancy in a Sears Tower match, Castor Strife gave it up to enter the World Title tournament, and Jack Bryant won the vacancy in a five-man ladder match. Its last chapter is a best-of-five series against Dorchester Stratton that the ledger tracks match by match and leaves with Stratton holding it.

events.note: Discontinued at the end of Futureshock and not reinstated until 16 May 2007, per the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).

name: NFW Triple Crown Championship
notes: Created by presidential order inside the fed's own fiction, announced at Supercrash IV and first awarded at Reloaded 11; the fed's own championship ledger records it only as the name the National Championship became.
epitaph: The last singles championship NFW made, and it was made by consolidation rather than by tournament: President Eddie Mayfield ordered the Pure, National and Elite Championships merged into one belt at Supercrash IV in January 2012, and Rook Black won it at Reloaded 11 that April by pinning Deacon in a three-way that also had the reigning Pure Champion in it. He carried it through the promotion's last touring year — Portland, the Gorge, Sydney, Helsinki — turning back the Mighty Impala, Akita and Leyenda de Ocho, and was still holding it at the last card the archive keeps.

name: NFW Ultratitle
notes: Transcribed from the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html). SOURCES DISAGREE about how long the Ultratitle ran. The fed's own championship ledger records two seasons and stops after Wrestlebowl II in May 2007; its own show text at Reloaded 13 and Reloaded 14 in 2012 twice refers to Castor Strife holding a 2012 Ultratitle Championship. Both readings are recorded; no third reign is written, because nothing in the served record stages one.
epitaph: Not a championship NFW made. The ULTRATITLE — an eight-tier trophy out of CSWA folklore — was donated to the fed when it rebuilt itself as a fantasy-sports league in 2003, and it was contested across a whole season rather than defended match to match: a draft lottery, two conferences, a sixteen-week regular season on a points table, wild cards, single-elimination playoffs and a Wrestlebowl. Michael Manson beat Shane Southern for Season One at Wrestlebowl I in North Charleston in January 2005. Nova beat Yori Yakamo Jr. for Season Two at Wrestlebowl II in Dallas in May 2007. The fed's own ledger heads the section "NFW Ultratitle Championship (2003-2007)" and records no third season.

name: NFW World Heavyweight Championship
notes: Transcribed from the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).
epitaph: NFW's own top belt for the whole of its run, and the one prize the Ultratitle never replaced. Bloodhunt was the inaugural champion, beating Ricky Zane at Crash 3 in Baltimore in October 2000 after both men won a thirty-man Random Rumble. Zane took it off him at Banned 4 Life in an angle the ledger records in one word — "Zanegate!" — and the belt then went through the fed's own messiest stretch: Rick Ryconik held it for nothing at all, beaten on the night by Armando Montezuma in a pin Commissioner Michael Manson ruled questionable enough to hold the title up, and Shane Southern won the vacancy in a fourway at Crash 8. Bloodhunt's second reign ended with the title defunct from August 2003 until Manson reinstated it in April 2004 and then won it himself. After that it settled: Doc Silver, Felix Red, Kin Hiroshi — who forfeited it by walking out of a threeway at Crash 43 — Dan Ryan, Nova, and Joe The Plumber, whose 860 days are the longest reign on the ledger, ended when President Eddie Mayfield suspended him for refusing a drug test. Castor Strife won the vacancy in a four-man tournament and lost it to Impulse in a scaffold match billed as The Cutting Room Floor. The ledger's own last word leaves Impulse reigning.

events.note: The ledger records the title defunct from 15 August 2003 until NFW East Commissioner Michael Manson reinstated it on 1 April 2004. (The ledger's own dates disagree with themselves here: the reign it attaches the note to opens 15 August 2002. Both readings are recorded rather than smoothed.) Per the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).

name: NFW World Tag Team Championship
notes: Transcribed from the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).
epitaph: NFW's tag championship, renamed the Everette Memorial Tag Team Championship when it returned in 2008 — for Avery Everette, the figure the fed's own history names as the first owner of the UWA, the Prodigy-era federation NFW says it grew out of. The Showstoppers were the inaugural champions, beating The Oblivion Express and Hellmachine in a three-way dance at Crash 5 on Christmas Day 2000. Hellmachine took the belts at Banned 4 Life and held them 440 days; The Original Showstoppers won a six-team playoff at Futureshock in August 2002 and the titles were retired at the end of that night, unreinstated until Supercrash I in February 2008. The Hollywood Wrecking Crew won the renamed belts in a tournament, and the ledger's own last reign is the Superfly Express, who beat Jack Bryant and Malik Anderson in the final of the Avery Cup.

events.note: Discontinued at the end of Futureshock and not reinstated until 15 February 2008, when they returned renamed the Everette Memorial Tag Team Championships, per the fed's own championship ledger (promotions/nfw/archive/a-guide-to-nfw-championship-history.html).

name: NFW Eastern Conference Championship
notes: Crowned once in the surviving record, on NFW's own served card of 15 March 2007, feeding the Ultratitle Final at Wrestlebowl II.
epitaph: The prize for winning NFW's own Eastern half of the 2007 Ultratitle playoffs, crowned by the ring announcer on the spot rather than staged as a title with a history behind it — the fed's own text does not say whether the belt existed before this show or who, if anyone, held it previously. Yori Yakamo Jr. no-sold a second Kooter Cruise chokeslam, bodyslammed him onto Felix Red, and pinned Red with the Yori=Awesome to become the first and, in the surviving record, only NFW Eastern Conference Champion, earning the berth against the Western Conference's own champion at Wrestlebowl.

name: NFW Western Conference Championship
notes: Crowned once in the surviving record, on NFW's own served card of 15 March 2007, feeding the Ultratitle Final at Wrestlebowl II.
epitaph: The prize for winning NFW's own Western half of the 2007 Ultratitle playoffs, run the same day as its Eastern counterpart. After a double count-out through a ringside table tied the match at a fall apiece, a barbed-wire cage went up for the decisive third fall; Nova came out of it the first-ever NFW Western Conference Champion, earning the berth against Eastern Conference Champion Yori Yakamo Jr. at Wrestlebowl. The same card's undercard staged a separate, unrelated Asylum Immortal Championship prize on a hook above the ring — recorded on that outside promotion's own frontier row, not here.

name: UWA World Heavyweight Championship
notes: Staged inside NFW's own continuity as a revival of the real UWA's own vacant, never-resolved World Championship (see that title's own record, uwa-world) — an in-fiction storyline device, not a claim that the real 1992–1997 Philadelphia UWA continued operating. Crowned across two of NFW's own served cards, Wrestlebowl I (31 Jan 2005) and Midnight Madness 5 (18 Nov 2005).
epitaph:
At Wrestlebowl I (31 January 2005), Avery Prosser — fresh off seizing NFW's own North division with his “Seven Deadly Sins” — produced the real UWA's own vacant World Championship belt on air and declared he would “RESURRECT this title” in the name of the man he called its rightful champion, presenting it to Troy Windham as “your DIVINE RIGHT.” Windham, taking the mic, claimed sole credit for having “MADE the UWA” seven years earlier. It was a political gift, not the result of a contest, and it did not survive the night: in the brawl that followed, Craig Miles pulled the belt off the fallen Windham and handed it to Tom Adler, and NFW's own text leaves the title “held up/vacant” for the rest of the season.

It came to a decision at Midnight Madness 5 (18 November 2005): Adler won the vacant title from Windham by disqualification, after Zoltan and August De La Rossi interfered and Windham sprayed him with an unspecified liquid — and Adler surrendered it within minutes, in the very next segment, picking up a microphone and saying only “I Quit” before handing it to Eddie Mayfield without further contest. Mayfield held it through two more defenses in the surviving record without it changing hands again: a no-contest against Eli Flair at UWA Pirate TV (24 December 2005), and a no-decision against Adler at Wrestlestock I (20 April 2006). No later NFW document shows the belt again.

The prop is staged throughout as the same belt the real UWA left vacant in 1997, not a new one — commentary calls it a title “resurrected... for this season,” and Windham's own promo reaches back to that history directly. The real UWA's own ledger (uwa-world) records only what its own 1992–1997-era evidence supports; this row holds NFW's later fiction about it.

name: UWA Women's World Championship
notes: Attested entirely inside NFW's own served corpus, which stages the UWA as a hub-adjacent outside promotion rather than holding it directly; a news article on the same corpus says the belt was renamed after Lucky Seven won an “inaugural SLICE-USA Grand Prix,” a predecessor lineage this collection holds no document for. Filed under NFW rather than the real (1992–1997) UWA: unlike the men's World title, no document here ties this belt to that promotion's own record or its known 1990s roster, and it may or may not be the same in-fiction “resurrected UWA” NFW staged for the men's title (nfw-uwa-world) — the record does not say either way.
epitaph: Lucky Seven is the only champion this record ever names, and she is already carrying the belt the one time it surfaces: an NFW-billed unification bout at Brawl 62 in Berlin, her own in-ring NFW debut, where she defeats Pan-Euro Women's Champion Dani “Alpha” Engel to fold that title into hers. No document held here stages how or when she won it, or whether the “UWA” it names is the same 1990s Philadelphia promotion or NFW's own later storyline revival of it.

name: NFW Grand Prix
epitaph: A tournament NFW ran three times. Doctor Curiosity won the first, a three-way elimination bout at Supercrash II in October 2008, Legion the 2011 edition at its Monaco final, and Jack Harmen the 2013 edition, which earned him a shot at the NFW World Heavyweight Championship.

name: Great American Smokeout Bunkhouse Championship
epitaph: A one-night Bunkhouse Stampede eliminator, closed by a War Games segment among its final three, which the fed itself named a championship. Captain Justice won it at Crash TV 50 on 29 August 2009, its one recorded winner.

name: NFW Conference Regular Season Championship
epitaph: The crown for finishing first in an NFW conference's regular season, won by clinching the conference's first seed for the Ultratitle playoffs. The fed's own shows name the East, North and South champions of Season One in 2004, and the Eastern champion of Season Two.

name: NFW Hulk-a-Thon
epitaph: NFW's Hulk-A-Thon, billed as the first annual: a fifteen-entrant tournament of triple-threat elimination rounds whose five winners met in a War Games-style cage. Yori Yakamo, Jr. won it at Midnight Madness 8, Venice Beach, on 18 March 2006; the next one planned was cancelled.
notes: Billed on the night as "THE FIRST ANNUAL SYMPOSIUM OF THE IMMORTAL HULKAMANIA"; the next Hulk-A-Thon, announced for 2007, was cancelled on air at Crash TV 42 (28 November 2007).
